summary: This paper studies Mamba's in-context learning (ICL) capabilities through the lens of random Markov chains, showing empirically that a single-layer Mamba learns the optimal Laplacian smoothing estimator and identifying convolution as the key enabling component. A constructive theoretical proof (Theorem 1) establishes that a simplified model, MambaZero, can exactly represent the Laplacian estimator for first-order Markov processes, and a complementary lower bound (Theorem 2) shows recurrent architectures require exponentially large hidden dimension for k-th order chains. The work is the first to apply the Markov-ICL framework to Mamba and provides a rare constructive theory-practice alignment, but the central theorem is confined to first-order chains while the abstract and title claim 'all Markov orders,' and the tension between the exponential lower bound and empirical higher-order success is insufficiently resolved.
strengths: Genuinely novel theoretical contribution: the constructive proof of Theorem 1 aligns tightly with empirically observed parameter structure (a_t ≈ 1, selective b/c inner-product nulling), making it unusually grounded and interpretable.

Clean ablation identifying convolution as the key component, supported by both the synthetic Markov experiments (Fig. 3a) and cross-architectural WikiText-103 experiments (Table 1), with consistent directionality.
Theorem 2 provides a non-trivial information-theoretic lower bound on recurrent hidden dimension for Laplacian smoothing, applicable to any recurrent architecture regardless of depth.
The switching Markov experiment (Sec. 5.1) elegantly isolates the selectivity gate a_t and shows it functioning as a context-reset mechanism, going meaningfully beyond the Markovian regime.
First application of the Markov-ICL framework to Mamba/SSMs, enabling apples-to-apples comparison with the transformer literature that developed this framework.

key_concerns.issue: The abstract, introduction, and Figure 1 caption claim single-layer Mamba learns the optimal Laplacian estimator 'for all Markov orders,' but Theorem 1 covers only first-order chains. Higher-order support is empirical only (Fig. 1b), and extending the construction to k > 1 appears non-trivial given the window-size and count-tracking arguments. This is a systematic overstatement of the theoretical contribution.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Explicitly and prominently delineate in the abstract/intro that the theoretical result is first-order only and that higher-order cases are empirical. Either extend Theorem 1 to general k (perhaps with a looser constructive bound), or retitle/reframe the contribution as a first-order theory with higher-order empirical evidence.

key_concerns.issue: Theorem 2 asserts d·p ≥ 2^k(1−3ε)log(1/ε), implying exponentially large hidden dimension for higher-order Laplacian approximation. Yet empirically, a fixed-size single-layer Mamba works for k = 1,...,4 (Fig. 1b). The paper asserts this comparison 'provides context' but does not reconcile the apparent contradiction. Are the empirical models' hidden dimensions large enough to satisfy the bound for k = 4? What value of ε do they effectively achieve?
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Include a brief quantitative check: report the hidden dimension d and precision p of the trained models, compute the lower bound for each k tested, and explicitly state whether the empirical models satisfy or violate the bound (and at what effective ε). This either validates the bound is non-vacuous or reveals an interesting gap.

key_concerns.issue: The natural language experiments (Table 1, WikiText-103) contain only four rows with no variance/error bars across runs, making it impossible to determine whether the perplexity differences are statistically significant. The 11% perplexity improvement for Mamba with convolution is headline-worthy but unsupported by any significance estimate.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report mean ± std over at least 3 seeds for Table 1, or provide confidence intervals. At minimum, note that the experiment was run once and flag the limitation.

key_concerns.issue: The entire theoretical analysis (Theorems 1 and 2) is for MambaZero, not full Mamba. The reduction relies on the empirical claim that convolution is sufficient (Fig. 3a), but this equivalence is never formally stated or proved. A reader cannot determine from the theory alone whether the full Mamba (with gating, MLP, ReLU) has strictly greater or strictly equal representation power relative to MambaZero for this task.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a brief formal proposition or remark explicitly stating the relationship between MambaZero and full Mamba for the Laplacian representation task, even if only a one-directional containment argument.

key_concerns.issue: The comparison 'Mamba requires exponential hidden dimension (Thm. 2) whereas transformers need linear dimension (Rajaraman et al., 2024)' conflates a lower bound for one architecture class with an upper bound (construction) for another. This is not an apples-to-apples comparison and risks misleading readers about relative expressivity.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Clarify that Thm. 2 is a lower bound for recurrent models and the transformer result is an upper bound (construction), and note that a matching recurrent upper bound or a transformer lower bound is needed for a fair comparison.

questions_for_authors: Can Theorem 1 be extended to kth-order Markov chains (k > 1) with a hidden dimension that grows polynomially in k? The window-size argument in Sec. 4.2 suggests w ≥ k+1 is sufficient empirically — does the counting construction generalize directly?

For the trained models evaluated in Fig. 1b (orders k = 2, 3, 4), what are the hidden dimension d and numerical precision p? Does the product d·p satisfy the lower bound of Theorem 2 for the observed effective approximation error ε?

Figure 3b shows the model requires w ≥ k+1 to learn order-k chains. Is there a corresponding result showing that w = k+1 is also necessary (not just sufficient)? The paper says 'one can find confusable sequences' but this seems like a full necessity argument — can it be stated as a theorem?

In the WikiText-103 ablations (Table 1 and Appendix E.8), how sensitive are the results to model size? The paper notes that relative convolution importance decreases with depth (Table 5 in appendix) — does this trend continue to the point where convolution becomes irrelevant in large models, and if so, does it challenge the Markov-to-language generalization argument?

For the switching Markov experiment (Sec. 5.1), what is the L1 distance from the optimal reset estimator (the one that resets counts at each switch)? Tracking a_t qualitatively is suggestive, but a quantitative comparison analogous to Fig. 1b would strengthen the claim.
calibration_check: The empirical claims ('all Markov orders') substantially outrun the theoretical claims (first-order only), and the lower bound of Theorem 2 is presented as a Mamba disadvantage without reconciling it against the empirical higher-order successes; the authors acknowledge the gap in places but the title, abstract, and key-contribution list consistently imply broader theoretical coverage than is delivered.

significance.justification: First theoretical grounding of Mamba's ICL through the Laplacian estimator is a meaningful contribution to the growing SSM theory literature, with practical implications for understanding when and why Mamba succeeds.

novelty.justification: The Markov-ICL framework had not previously been applied to SSMs; the identification of convolution as the key ICL-enabling component and the constructive Laplacian representation proof are genuinely new results.

rigor.justification: Theorem 1's constructive proof is sound and notably grounded in empirically verified parameter structure, but the scope is limited to first-order chains and the theory-to-full-Mamba reduction relies on unformalized empirical equivalence arguments.

statistical_soundness.justification: Only 5 seeds for synthetic experiments with standard deviation reported is marginal; no variance reported for WikiText-103 results; no significance tests for any claim, and the headline 11% perplexity improvement lacks uncertainty quantification.

calibration_honesty.justification: The abstract and figure captions claim optimality 'for all Markov orders' while the theorem covers only first-order, and the lower bound versus empirical performance tension is unresolved; the paper acknowledges gaps but the framing consistently overstates the theoretical scope.

clarity.justification: The narrative flow from empirical observation to theoretical construction to proof sketch is logical and well-paced; the MambaZero simplification is clearly motivated; minor clarity issues arise from dense recurrence equations that are harder to parse in text form.

structure_compliance.justification: Follows standard conference structure with appropriate section balance; Conclusion is appropriately brief and honest about future work; length appears consistent with ICLR norms.

reproducibility.justification: Theorem 1 specifies exact dimensions (N=S, d=2S, e=1, w=2) which is good; experimental hyperparameters are deferred to appendix F; the reliance on appendices for most experimental detail is acceptable but the main text gives insufficient specifics for a first-pass reproduction attempt.

related_work.justification: Coverage of SSM/Mamba expressivity literature and ICL-for-transformers literature is solid; the paper correctly positions itself as complementary to comparative empirical studies and as extending the Markov-ICL framework; the Mamba vs. transformer lower-versus-upper-bound comparison issue is a positioning gap.

figure_quality.justification: From captions, Fig. 1 directly measures L1 deviation from the optimal estimator across Markov orders — an ideal metric for the claim; Fig. 3 isolates convolution via ablation and links window size to Markov order; the captions are sufficiently detailed to evaluate the display items.

breadth_generality.justification: Theory covers only first-order Markov chains; natural language experiments are limited to a single dataset with four model variants and no error bars; higher-order claims rest entirely on empirical Fig. 1b without analysis of the approximation quality.

overall_recommendation.justification: Borderline accept: the paper has a genuine theoretical core, an interesting empirical discovery, and a well-motivated framework, but the calibration gap between abstract claims and actual theorems, the unresolved tension with the lower bound for higher orders, and the thin NLP experiments collectively prevent a clear accept without revisions.
